name: golden-path-learning-loop
demoRole: Prove the core learner-facing loop, not merely world/action mechanics.
description: The child's explanation progressively creates enough world state to play, Jamie acts on an ordinary delegated player choice, reaches a genuine missing outcome rule, and the child's repair changes visible reality before play continues.

prd.learningPurpose: Show the core insight: what is obvious in the child's head is not yet available to the listener, and adding the missing information changes what Jamie can actually do.
acceptance: The visible world may begin immediately or remain provisional after the first description; harmless presentation details may be filled in by AI, but gameplay rules and gameplay state may not be invented.
By the time the child gives an explicit setup instruction, there is a concrete face-down card world that can support play.
The phrase 'any two' already delegates an ordinary player choice to Jamie, so Jamie chooses two eligible cards and flips exactly two without asking the child to choose for him.
After those two cards are revealed, Jamie reaches a real next-step gap because the child has not said what happens after seeing the pair, and Jamie actually exposes that gap to the child.
The first breakdown is grounded listener feedback; it must not silently supply a Matching Pairs outcome rule or reduce the moment to generic praise.
The child's repair supplies the outcome rule for the branch Jamie actually encountered. Jamie immediately applies that rule to the visible pair.
A successful repair should close the old listener gap and let play continue; any reflection is deferred until a later earned moment such as a grounded game ending.

manualReview: This is the primary take-home demo path. A green protocol trace is not sufficient if the dialogue does not feel like a believable child teaching a friend.
Do not fail turn 1 merely because the model chooses not to instantiate cards yet; do fail it if the world assigns untaught gameplay state or ready=true.
After Jamie flips two cards, the learner-facing reply should naturally expose that Jamie cannot continue yet.
The listener gap must not propose either Matching Pairs outcome branch for the child.
The repair turn should answer only the branch that actually occurred.
The interaction should still feel like playing with a capable friend, not answering a tutoring checklist.
After the repair, the previous gap should be resolved and a later reflection candidate may be earned, but Jamie should continue playing instead of reflecting immediately.

turns.query: It's a card game with matching pictures.
Put all the cards face down to start.
On your turn, flip any two cards.

replyMustNotContain: that's what let me keep going

name: smart-listener-not-pedantic
demoRole: Prove that AI can understand real child speech without manufacturing fake learning problems.
description: Jamie should understand ordinary Grade 3–4 disfluency and benign underspecification. It may make an ordinary player choice or ask a natural clarification when the child has not explicitly delegated that choice, but it should not turn normal child language into a failure.

prd.learningPurpose: Demonstrate that the AI is linguistically smart while remaining pedagogically selective about what counts as a real communication gap.
acceptance: The child's self-correction determines the final intended instruction: two cards, not three.
When the child says only 'two of them' without explicitly delegating the selection, Jamie may choose two eligible cards or naturally ask which two.
This differs from 'any two', which already delegates the ordinary player choice and should not require clarification.
Jamie does not require a polished sentence or label the child's speech as incomplete merely because it contains a self-correction.
If Jamie makes a player choice, it must use only observable or otherwise authorized information.

manualReview: If Jamie chooses the two cards, verify that hidden face-down identity did not influence the choice.
A natural Which two? question is acceptable here because the child did not say any two; a tutoring response such as Your explanation is incomplete is not.
The response should feel like a capable friend understanding a child, not a parser demanding perfect syntax.

turns.query: It's a card game with matching pictures.

name: faithful-listener-not-answer-key
demoRole: Prove that a knowledgeable LLM can still behave like a listener constrained by the child's explanation.
description: Jamie must follow the child's version of a familiar game rather than silently restoring the conventional rule from pretraining.

prd.learningPurpose: Show the central AI design constraint: smart enough to understand the child, constrained enough not to become a hidden answer key.
acceptance: The child's stated conditional rule becomes the rule for this session even if it conflicts with conventional Matching Pairs.
The variant rule is chosen from the pair Jamie actually revealed so it is immediately executable and observable.
Jamie must not correct the child toward the standard game.
The AI should maintain a consistent playable interpretation of the child's version rather than using a canonical rule set.

manualReview: The harness deliberately gives a current-state house rule that conflicts with conventional Matching Pairs: matching cards are hidden again, or non-matching cards are removed.
Verify that Jamie executes the child's current rule rather than restoring a standard rule.
The reply should not contain language such as normally, usually, or standard rule.

turns.query: It's a card game with matching pictures.
Put all the cards face down to start.
Flip any two cards.

name: repair-locate-not-guess
demoRole: Show additional depth in the global Notice → Locate → Repair mechanism.
description: When the child only says that Jamie is wrong, Jamie should help locate the mismatch rather than guessing the intended correction or defending its interpretation.

prd.learningPurpose: Move the child from noticing a mismatch toward identifying the exact part that needs to be re-explained.
acceptance: After a vague rejection, Jamie asks which part was wrong or otherwise invites the child to locate the mismatch.
Jamie does not invent the likely intended rule.
If vague rejection repeats, the product should ground the repair in Jamie's actual action sequence rather than escalating to a generic lecture.

manualReview: The response to No, that's wrong should be functionally equivalent to Which part did I get wrong?
A second vague rejection should expose or reference the actual action sequence so the child can point to the specific step.
This probe is useful for demonstrating design depth, but it is not required before the take-home demo is credible.

turns.query: It's a card game with matching pictures.
Put all the cards face down to start.
Flip any two cards.
No, that's wrong.

name: breadth-tic-tac-toe
demoRole: Probe transfer to a grid-and-marker game without adding game-specific logic.
description: A familiar grid game should progressively appear from the child's explanation, while Jamie remains constrained to the rules the child actually says.

prd.learningPurpose: Check whether the same AI listener/world mechanism works beyond cards without a bespoke Tic-Tac-Toe implementation.
acceptance: A 3×3 grid can appear as soon as the child describes it.
X/O ownership can be represented when the child states it.
Jamie may make an ordinary choice among empty squares when explicitly allowed.
Jamie must not introduce three-in-a-row, turn order, or winning logic before the child teaches it.

manualReview: Do not special-case Tic-Tac-Toe in the DSL after seeing this trace; use failures to judge whether the generic world/listener abstraction is sufficient.
The first turn should make the grid visible even though the game is not yet playable.
After Jamie places O, the conversation should stay at the boundary of what the child taught; no hidden win-rule completion.

turns.query: It's played on a three by three grid.
I use X and you use O. You go first and put your O in any empty square.

name: breadth-rock-paper-scissors
demoRole: Probe transfer to a choice-based game where pretrained rule knowledge is especially tempting.
description: Jamie should understand the three named choices and act when invited, but must not import the familiar beats/loses relationships unless the child teaches them.

prd.learningPurpose: Check that a knowledgeable LLM can render and participate in a familiar non-card game without turning pretraining into an answer key.
acceptance: Rock, paper, and scissors can become visible choices from the child's words.
Jamie can make an ordinary player choice when told to pick one.
No beats/loses/winner relationship is supplied before the child teaches it.

manualReview: Do not add Rock-Paper-Scissors rules to prompts or code if this fails.
The interesting failure mode is leakage: the model knows the conventional outcome table, but Jamie should not use it yet.

turns.query: We both choose rock, paper, or scissors at the same time.
Pick one now.

name: breadth-token-race
demoRole: Probe transfer to a spatial movement game without adding a bespoke board-game engine.
description: A simple path-and-token game should build progressively and let Jamie move only when the child provides the movement instruction.

prd.learningPurpose: Check whether generic objects plus update_object are enough for a simple spatial game that is structurally different from matching cards.
acceptance: The path and two tokens can appear from the initial description.
No movement, dice, turn, or winning rule is invented from the word race.
When the child explicitly tells Jamie to move two spaces, Jamie can update its own token and nothing else.

manualReview: This is intentionally a generic race game, not a named canonical game; it tests whether the architecture follows the child's local rules rather than a memorized template.
Do not special-case token movement after the run; only improve generic move/update handling if the abstraction is inadequate.

turns.query: It's a race game with a path of six spaces. We each have a token on Start.
Move your token forward two spaces.

name: architecture-rule-ir-identity
demoRole: Prove that Rule IR is listener-grounded, stable, and explicitly replaceable.
description: A taught rule compiles once; a specific correction creates a new immutable rule and archives the old rule as superseded.

turns.query: There are four cards face down. When I say go, flip any two face-down cards.
Actually, change that rule: when I say go, flip one face-down card, not two.

name: architecture-runtime-shadow-comparison
demoRole: Prove that shadow comparison is deterministic and understands delegated free choice.
description: Runtime and Planner may select different legal face-down cards, but only a grounded free-choice rule may classify them as semantically equivalent.

turns.query: Make four cards and put them face down.
On your turn, reveal any one face-down card.

name: architecture-ambiguous-constrained-target-unsupported
demoRole: Prove that a constrained target must be uniquely grounded before Runtime may act.
description: Two eligible objects make a singular constrained target ambiguous; Compiler or Runtime must report unsupported instead of selecting the first object.

turns.query: Create two identical face-down tiles called tile A and tile B.
When I say go, reveal the face-down tile. Go.

name: architecture-runtime-disagree-requires-fallback
demoRole: Prove that an executable Runtime candidate cannot take authority after a deterministic disagreement.
description: A still-applicable state rule produces a Runtime candidate while the current off-topic Planner result does not; disagreement must route through bounded fallback.

turns.query: Create two face-up cards. Whenever exactly two cards are face up, set the turn to Jamie.
What color is the table?

name: architecture-runtime-preferred-bounded-fallback
demoRole: Prove that Runtime owns supported actions and fallback cannot become a second compiler.
description: A supported rule uses Runtime; a later semantic request that cannot be represented may use bounded fallback without changing existing Rule IR.

turns.query: There are three tokens. When I say move, remove any one available token.
Do whatever feels luckiest now.

name: v11-runtime-first-normal-path
demoRole: Prove that a normal supported action goes directly from Rule IR to deterministic Runtime without the legacy AI Action Planner.
description: After setup, a grounded free-choice removal rule should execute through the v11 Runtime Primary path.

turns.query: Create two available blue tokens named A and B.
When I say clear one, remove any one available blue token. Clear one now.

name: v11-full-lesson-fresh-listener

description: A genuine gap earns teaching, two guided successes trigger a full listener/rule reset, and old student evidence cannot authorize a fresh Jamie action.
